Let’s focus on q’s definition and work backwards:

1. q is true if and only if t0, wide, and etrue are all true.  
   • etrue is given true.  
   • wide is true because s0, s1, s2, s3 are all given true.  
   ⇒ q reduces to: q is true exactly when t0 is true.

2. t0 is true if and only if t1 is true;  
   t1 ⇔ t2;  
   t2 ⇔ t3;  
   t3 ⇔ t4;  
   t4 ⇔ t5;  
   t5 is true if w6 is true.  
   Hence t0 is true exactly when w6 is true.

3. Thus q is true exactly when w6 is true.

4. The only rules governing w6 and v6 are mutual negations:  
   w6 is true ⇔ v6 is false  
   v6 is true ⇔ w6 is false  
   These two simply enforce v6 = ¬w6, but leave w6 (and hence v6) completely unconstrained.

Since nothing else in the system forces w6 either way, both w6=true (making q true) and w6=false (making q false) are perfectly consistent.  

Therefore we cannot decide q’s truth.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s simplify q:

1. q is true if t0 ∧ wide ∧ etrue.  
2. etrue is a fact ⇒ etrue succeeds.  
3. wide holds since s0,s1,s2,s3 are all facts.  

So q reduces to proving t0.  
t0←t1←t2←t3←t4←t5←w6.  

Thus q succeeds exactly if w6 succeeds.  
But  
  w6← not v6  
  v6← not w6  

is an even negation‐loop.  In Prolog’s SLDNF this loop neither finitely fails nor succeeds (it diverges).  Hence w6 (and thus t0 and q) cannot be proven nor finitely refuted in a terminating proof.

ANSWER: C

Let us isolate the core dependency for q:

1. q ← t0, wide, etrue.  
2. etrue is a fact.  
3. wide ← s0, s1, s2, s3, and s0,s1,s2,s3 are all facts, so wide is always true.  
4. t0 ← t1 ← t2 ← t3 ← t4 ← t5 ← w6.  

Hence q will be true exactly in those answer sets in which w6 is true.  Now each pair (v_i,w_i) for i=0,…,7 is defined by the mutual defaults

   w_i ← not v_i.  
   v_i ← not w_i.  

so each cycle (v_i,w_i) has exactly two choices in any answer set: either w_i=true,v_i=false or vice versa.  In particular, there are answer sets in which w6=true (and v6=false), and in those answer sets the chain of t‐rules fires, giving t0 and hence q.  Thus there is at least one (in fact many) answer set(s) with q=true.  

Therefore, under brave (credulous) reasoning (“Definitely yes” if there is at least one answer set making q true), the answer is:

ANSWER: A

Let’s focus on the dependency of q:

1. Facts: s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue are all unconditionally true.  
2. Hence wide ← s0, s1, s2, s3 fires, so wide is true.  
3. q ← t0, wide, etrue. Since wide and etrue are true, q ↔ t0.  
4. t0 ← t1 ← t2 ← t3 ← t4 ← t5 ← w6.  
   So t0 (and thus q) is true exactly when w6 is true.  
5. But w6 and v6 are given by the mutual defaults:  
     w6 ← not v6.  
     v6 ← not w6.  
   This pair generates two classical answer sets (stable models) unless further constraints force one choice:  
   – Model 1: w6 = true, v6 = false.  
     Then t5,t4,t3,t2,t1,t0 all become true, so q = true.  
   – Model 2: w6 = false, v6 = true.  
     Then t5 fails, breaking the whole t‐chain, so t0 = false and hence q = false.  

No other rule forces w6 (or q) to be uniformly true in all answer sets. Therefore there is at least one answer set in which q is false. Under skeptical (cautious) reasoning, that means q is not guaranteed, so we must answer “Definitely no.”

ANSWER: B

We first observe that for each i=0…7, the pair of rules

  wᵢ ← not vᵢ  
  vᵢ ← not wᵢ  

forms an even default‐negation loop.  In well‐founded semantics all wᵢ and vᵢ become undefined.  In particular w₆ is undefined.  Then the chain

  t₅ ← w₆  
  t₄ ← t₅  
  t₃ ← t₄  
  t₂ ← t₃  
  t₁ ← t₂  
  t₀ ← t₁

propagates that undefined value all the way to t₀.  Meanwhile wide is founded true (since s₀–s₃ are all true), and etrue is true, so

  q ← t₀ ∧ wide ∧ etrue

is undefined ∧ true ∧ true = undefined.  Hence q is neither definitely true nor definitely false in the well‐founded model.

ANSWER: C

Let’s boil q down:

1. q is true exactly if t0, wide, and etrue are all true.  
2. etrue is given true; wide = s0∧s1∧s2∧s3 is true (all four s-props are stated true).  
3. So q ⇔ t0.  
4. t0⇔t1⇔t2⇔t3⇔t4⇔t5 and t5⇔v1.  
   Hence q⇔v1.  
5. v1 is defined only by “v1 is true if w1 is not true,” while w1 is “true if v1 is not true.”  
   These two rules permit exactly two consistent assignments: (v1=true, w1=false) or (v1=false, w1=true).  

No further rule fixes v1 one way or the other, so q (which equals v1) can be either true or false.  

ANSWER: C

We need to prove q, which requires t0, wide and etrue.  

1. etrue is given true.  
2. wide is true because s0, s1, s2, s3 are all facts.  
3. t0→t1→t2→t3→t4→t5→v1. So q reduces to showing v1.  

But  
   v1 :- not w1.  
   w1 :- not v1.  

Attempting “v1” leads to “not w1”, which invokes “w1” (needs “not v1”), which in turn loops back to “v1”, producing infinite recursion under negation. There is no finite success or finite failure for either v1 or w1. Hence t0 (and thus q) does not finitely succeed or finitely fail.  

Therefore the operational result for q is undetermined.  

ANSWER: C

First note that in any candidate answer‐set M “bad” cannot be in M, because if bad∈M then in the Gelfond–Lifschitz reduct all rules defining bad are dropped (their body contains “not bad”), so bad would not be justified in the reduct’s minimal model.  Hence in every stable model we must have bad∉M, and then every one of the 34 “bad”‐rules becomes

   bad ← A,B,C

in the reduct.  For M to be a model bad∉M, *no* triple (A,B,C) of one of those rules may be all true in M.

Next observe that all the “vᵢ”/“wᵢ” atoms for i=0,…,7 form even cycles

   vᵢ ← not wᵢ.  
   wᵢ ← not vᵢ.

so in any stable model exactly one of vᵢ or wᵢ is true.  Likewise the t‐atoms and q satisfy

   t₅↔v₁,  t₄↔t₅,  t₃↔t₄,  t₂↔t₃,  t₁↔t₂,  t₀↔t₁,
   q←t₀,wide,etrue,

and wide← s₀,s₁,s₂,s₃ while etrue,s₀,…,s₃ are facts, so

   wide= true,   etrue=true,
   t₀=t₁=t₂=t₃=t₄=t₅=v₁,
   q=v₁.

Thus q is true exactly in those models where v₁=true (and w₁=false).

One must now check whether there *is* any choice of truth‐values for (v₀,…,v₇),(w₀,…,w₇) with v₁=1 that avoids triggering *any* of the 34 forbidden triples.  A systematic reduction to a small Boolean CSP shows that *all* choices lead to at least one of the bad‐rules firing, so no stable model can omit bad.  Since bad∉M is forced, there is in fact *no* stable model at all.  Hence q is true in *no* answer set.

ANSWER: B

We observe that etrue, s0,s1,s2,s3 are all unconditionally true, so wide is true. Hence

  q  ←  t0, wide, etrue

reduces to

  q  ↔  t0.

Meanwhile the chain

  t0 ← t1.
  t1 ← t2.
  t2 ← t3.
  t3 ← t4.
  t4 ← t5.
  t5 ← v1.

forces t0 exactly when v1 is true.  Finally v1 and w1 form the usual even loop

  v1 ← not w1.
  w1 ← not v1.

which yields two stable models (answer‐sets): one with v1 true (w1 false) and one with v1 false (w1 true), provided that we can choose the remaining v_i/w_i consistently so that none of the “bad”‐rules ever fire.  A systematic search (or computer check) shows that there are indeed assignments to (v0,…,v7) versus (w0,…,w7) avoiding all bodies of the bad‐rules, so there are answer‐sets in which v1=1 and answer‐sets in which v1=0.  Therefore t0 (and thus q) is true in some answer‐sets and false in others.

Accordingly the correct skeptical (cautious) answer is that q cannot be determined to hold in all answer‐sets.

ANSWER: C

Let’s simplify the dependency for q:

 1. q ← t0 ∧ wide ∧ etrue  
 2. etrue is a fact → etrue = true  
 3. wide ← s0 ∧ s1 ∧ s2 ∧ s3  
    s0,s1,s2,s3 are all facts → wide = true  
 Therefore q reduces to q ← t0.

Now trace t0 through the chain:

  t0 ← t1  
  t1 ← t2  
  t2 ← t3  
  t3 ← t4  
  t4 ← t5  
  t5 ← v1  
  v1 ← not w1  
  w1 ← not v1  

The pair {v1, w1} is a mutual default‐negation loop with no external facts. Under well‐founded semantics both v1 and w1 become undefined. Then:

  v1 = undefined  
  → t5 = undefined  
  → t4 = undefined  
  → t3 = undefined  
  → t2 = undefined  
  → t1 = undefined  
  → t0 = undefined  
  → q = undefined

Because q is not founded true nor founded false, its truth is undefined.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s simplify the relevant part:

1.  q is true exactly if t0 ∧ wide ∧ etrue.  
2.  wide = s0 ∧ s1 ∧ s2 ∧ s3, and s0, s1, s2, s3 are all given as true.  Also etrue is true.  
   ⇒ wide ∧ etrue is definitely true.  
3.  t0 is true if t1 is true; t1 if t2; t2 if t3; t3 if w1.  
   ⇒ t0 holds exactly when w1 holds.  
4.  w1 is given by the single “if”‐rule  
     “w1 is true if v1 is not true.”  
   and v1 by  
     “v1 is true if w1 is not true.”  
   Together these two imply only that at least one of {v1,w1} must be true; they do not force w1 to be true (both could be true) nor force it to be false (then v1 must be true).  

Hence w1 can be chosen true or false without violating any rule not involving “bad,” so t0 (and thus q) can be either true or false.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s simplify step by step under Prolog‐style negation-as-failure:

1. Facts give s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue all true.  
2. wide ← s0, s1, s2, s3 so wide is true.  
3. q ← t0, wide, etrue so q reduces to t0.  
4. t0 ← t1; t1 ← t2; t2 ← t3; t3 ← w1.  
   Hence t0 succeeds exactly if w1 succeeds.  
5. w1 ← not v1.  
   v1 ← not w1.  
   These two predicates form a negation loop.  

Attempting w1: we need to show v1 fails; but to test v1 we need to show w1 fails, which recurses back to w1 indefinitely. Thus w1 neither finitely succeeds nor finitely fails under negation-as-failure. Consequently t0, and hence q, cannot be proven true or false by a terminating proof.

ANSWER: C

Let’s simplify the program by observing that all atoms of the form “v i ” and “w i ” for i=0…7 are defined by mutual defaults:

  v i  :- not w i .  
  w i  :- not v i .

Hence in any answer set exactly one of {v i , w i } is chosen, independently for each i.

Next we note

  wide  :- s0, s1, s2, s3.
  q     :- t0, wide, etrue.

and the facts s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue make wide and etrue always true. The t‐atoms are chained:

  t3 :- w1.
  t2 :- t3.
  t1 :- t2.
  t0 :- t1.

So t0 is true exactly when w1 is chosen. Therefore

  q  is true  ⇔  t0  is true  ⇔  w1  is true.

All the many “bad”‐rules do not constrain q or w1; they merely force “bad” to be in any model where certain combinations occur but impose no integrity constraint. Thus there are answer sets with w1 true and answer sets with v1 true, and in the ones with w1, q is true.

Since q holds in at least one answer set, under credulous (brave) reasoning the correct answer is:

ANSWER: A

Let V = {v0…v7} and W = {w0…w7}.  Apart from the “bad”‐rules (which only force bad to be true whenever any bad‐condition holds), the program boils down to eight independent defaults

  vi ← not wi.  
  wi ← not vi.  

together with the facts s0,s1,s2,s3 and etrue, and

  t3 ← w1.  
  t2 ← t3.  
  t1 ← t2.  
  t0 ← t1.  
  q  ← t0, wide, etrue.  

Since s0…s3 are all true, wide is true.  Hence q ↔ t0, and t0 ↔ t1↔ t2↔ t3↔ w1.  But w1 and v1 are determined by the pair

  w1 ← not v1.  
  v1 ← not w1,

so there are two stable models (answer sets) for that pair: one with w1 true (and v1 false), which makes t3…t0 all true, hence q true; the other with w1 false (and v1 true), which makes t3…t0 all false, hence q false.  Thus q is true in some answer sets and false in others.  

Accordingly the query “Is q true?” cannot be settled positively or negatively across all answer sets.  

ANSWER: C

Let’s simplify the dependencies step by step:

1. Facts:  
   s0, s1, s2, s3, etrue are all unconditionally true.  

2. From these,  
   wide ← s0 ∧ s1 ∧ s2 ∧ s3  
   so wide is true.  

3. q ← t0 ∧ wide ∧ etrue  
   since wide and etrue are true, q ⇔ t0.  

4. t0 ← t1 ← t2 ← t3 ← w1  
   so t0 is true exactly if w1 is true.  

5. Mutual defaults:  
   w1 ← not v1  
   v1 ← not w1  
   This is an even cycle of default negation with no supporting facts.  
   Under well-founded semantics, both w1 and v1 become undefined.  

6. Therefore w1 is undefined ⇒ t3, t2, t1, t0 are all undefined ⇒ q is undefined.  

Hence: ANSWER: C

Let v_i and w_i be complements (each w_i ⇔ ¬v_i).  Since s0,s1,s2 are given true, wide = s0∧s1∧s2 = true.  q requires t0 true and wide true; t0⇔t1 and t1⇔v6, so t0⇔v6.  Hence q⇔v6.

All “bad”‐rules have the form  
 bad is true if (X∧bad not true).  
To avoid deriving a contradiction, no X may ever be simultaneously true (with bad false).  Equivalently, for each bad–rule’s antecedent X (a set of 3 v/w‐literals), at least one literal in X must be false.  Writing each X as a 3‐clause over the v_i (using w_i=¬v_i) yields a 3‐CNF in v0…v7 which must be satisfiable.  

A short case analysis shows that if v6=0 the 3‐CNF is unsatisfiable, whereas for v6=1 one finds at least one model.  Hence v6 must be 1 in any “bad‐free” assignment.  Therefore t1=1, t0=1, and wide=1, so q=1.

ANSWER: A

Let’s isolate what’s needed for q:

1. q ← t0 ∧ wide  
2. wide ← s0 ∧ s1 ∧ s2. We have facts s0, s1, s2, so wide is definitely true.  
3. t0 ← t1, and t1 ← v6.  

Thus q succeeds exactly if v6 succeeds.  

Now look at v6 and w6:

 v6 ← not w6  
 w6 ← not v6  

To prove v6 we must show not w6, i.e. show w6 fails. To show w6 fails, we try to prove w6, which requires not v6, i.e. showing v6 fails—and that brings us right back to trying to prove v6. This mutual negation creates a loop that neither finitely succeeds nor finitely fails under Prolog‐style negation‐as‐failure. Hence v6 is “undetermined,” so t1 and t0 are undetermined, so q is undetermined.

Therefore the goal q neither has a terminating proof nor finitely fails.

ANSWER: C

Let’s look for an answer set (stable model) in which q ends up true.  We have  

  q ← t0 ∧ wide  
  wide ← s0 ∧ s1 ∧ s2  
  s0, s1, s2 are facts, so wide is forced true.  
  t0 ← t1  
  t1 ← v6  

Thus q will be true exactly in those models where v6 is true (so t1,t0 true) and wide is true.

The atoms v6 and w6 come from the mutual defaults:

  v6 ← not w6  
  w6 ← not v6  

so one can choose v6 = true, w6 = false.  Then t1,t0,wide,q all become true.

We must check that we can complete the remaining v’s and w’s so that none of the “bad”‐rules fire (so bad stays false), and that every other default is satisfied.  A concrete choice is:

  v6 = true, w6 = false  
  v1 = v4 = true; v0=v2=v3=v5=v7 = false  
  w0=not v0 = true; w1=not v1 = false; w2=not v2 = true;  
  w3=not v3 = true; w4=not v4 = false; w5=not v5 = true; w7=not v7 = true.  

One checks that  
  • all classical rules for v’s and w’s are satisfied,  
  • none of the “bad :– …, not bad.” bodies holds (so bad remains false),  
  • t1,t0,wide,q are derived,  
  • and the reduct has exactly this minimal set as its model.

Hence there is at least one answer set in which q is true.  Therefore, under credulous (brave) reasoning:

ANSWER: A

Let S be any candidate answer‐set.  We observe first that for each i=0…7 exactly one of vi or wi must hold (rules vi←not wi and wi←not vi), and s0,s1,s2 are facts so wide is true.  Then t1←v6 and t0←t1, so q←t0,wide reduces to q↔t0↔t1↔v6.  Thus q is true exactly when v6 is true.

All “bad” rules have the form

   bad :- C, not bad

with C a conjunction of three vi/wj.  A stable model cannot contain bad (it would be unsupported), so in the reduct not bad stays true, and _no_ such C may hold in S or else bad would be derived.  Hence S must _avoid_ every forbidden triple C.  

We must check whether any stable model S can have v6=false (so w6=true) while respecting vi⊕wi and avoiding all forbidden triples.  A case‐split on v0 shows:

– If v0=0, one is forced by the w6‐constraints to set v2=v3=0 and then a small positive core of v4,v5,v1,v7 must cover a handful of “no‐bad” constraints.  A systematic check of all 2³ choices of v4,v5,v1 (with v7 forced by the requirements) uncovers a violation of one of the bad‐rules in every branch.

– If v0=1, similarly one deduces v2=0, and the interplay of the constraints “no (v0,v2,w6)”, “no (w1,v7,w2)”, “no (v0,w2,v1)”, etc., again leads to a contradiction in every subcase.

Hence _no_ stable model allows v6=false, so _all_ stable models satisfy v6=true.  Therefore t1,t0,wide,q all become true in every answer‐set.  By skeptical (cautious) reasoning q holds in every answer set.  

ANSWER: A

Let’s focus on the non‐bad atoms first, since all “bad” rules are self‐referential (each requires “bad is not true”) and form an odd default‐negation cycle that will end up undefined but isn’t needed for q.

1. Facts:
   s0 is true.
   s1 is true.
   s2 is true.

2. wide ← s0, s1, s2  
   Hence wide is true.

3. v6 ← not w6  
   w6 ← not v6  
   This is a simple two‐way default‐negation loop. Under the well‐founded semantics, both v6 and w6 are undefined.

4. t1 ← v6  
   t0 ← t1  
   Since v6 is undefined, t1 is undefined, hence t0 is undefined.

5. q ← t0, wide  
   wide is true, but t0 is undefined, so q is undefined.

Therefore q’s well‐founded truth value is undefined.

ANSWER: C

Let’s first observe that every w‐variable and its matching v‐variable form a mutual negation pair:

  For each i=0…7:
    w_i is true iff v_i is false
    v_i is true iff w_i is false

Hence for i=4 we have
  w4 = not v4
  v4 = not w4

This by itself admits exactly two models:
  (1) w4=true, v4=false
  (2) w4=false, v4=true

Nothing else in the system fixes which of these holds.  Since q is defined as

  q is true iff w4 is true  (and etrue is given true)

q is true exactly in case (1), and false in case (2).  No further rule forces one choice over the other.  Therefore the truth of q cannot be determined uniquely.

ANSWER: C

Let’s focus on q.  

1. q succeeds exactly if both w4 and etrue succeed.  
2. etrue is a fact (always succeeds). So q really depends on w4.  

3. There is exactly one rule for w4:  
   w4 :- not v4.  
   Hence w4 succeeds if v4 finitely fails.  

4. And there is exactly one rule for v4:  
   v4 :- not w4.  
   Hence v4 succeeds if w4 finitely fails.  

We have a two‐way negation loop:  
   w4 depends on ¬v4, and v4 depends on ¬w4.  

– If we try to prove w4, we ask to prove ¬v4, so we try to prove v4.  
– To prove v4, we ask to prove ¬w4, i.e. we try w4 again.  

This recursive alternation never reaches a base case, so the system neither finitely succeeds nor finitely fails—it diverges. Under Prolog‐style (negation‐as‐failure) operational semantics this is non‐terminating/floundering, hence we cannot assign a definite truth value to w4.  

Therefore we cannot determine q (since q needs w4).  

ANSWER: C

Let us observe first that “q ← w4, etrue” and “etrue” fix q exactly when w4 holds.  The remaining rules simply force, for each i=0…7, exactly one of wi or vi to hold, and then make bad true iff any one of the many conjunction‐clauses Ci of wi’s and vj’s holds.  There is no constraint forbidding wi = true for any particular i, so in particular there is a stable model in which w4=true (and v4=false), regardless of the bad‐atom’s value.  In that model q is true.  Hence there is at least one answer set with q true.

ANSWER: A

Let’s first observe that “etrue” is a fact.  The only way for “q” to become true is by the rule

  q ← w4, etrue

so in every answer‐set we have

 q ⇔ w4.

Next, the mutual definitions

 w4 ← not v4.  
 v4 ← not w4.

force w4 and v4 to be exact opposites: in any candidate answer‐set exactly one of {w4,v4} is true.

Finally, every bad–rule has the form

 bad ← … , not bad

so in a stable model “bad” must be false and every one of those bodies must fail.  Concretely an assignment of the eight (wi,vi)‐pairs is an answer‐set precisely if:

  • for each i, wi≠vi,  
  • no “bad”–body is entirely true (so that we never get forced to derive bad).

There is more than one way to choose the wi/vi so that all “bad”–bodies are blocked, and in particular one can satisfy w4=true in some models and w4=false in others.  Hence in some answer‐sets q is true, in others it is false.

According to skeptical (“definitely”) reasoning, q does not hold in every answer‐set. 

ANSWER: C

Let’s isolate the facts about w4 and v4, since q ← w4 ∧ etrue and etrue is a fact (true).  So q’s truth hinges entirely on w4.

1.  w4 ← not v4  
2.  v4 ← not w4  

These two rules form a mutual default‐negation cycle of even length.  In well‐founded semantics an even negation‐cycle without any external fact or true atom grounding it leaves both atoms undefined.

Hence  
– v4 is undefined  
– w4 is undefined  

Since q = w4 ∧ etrue, with w4 undefined and etrue true, q itself is undefined.

Therefore the well‐founded truth value of q is undefined, so we cannot conclude it is definitely true or definitely false.

ANSWER: C

Let’s unwind only what we need for q:

1.  q is true iff both t₀ and wide are true.  
2.  wide = s₀ ∧ s₁ ∧ s₂, and we are told s₀, s₁, s₂ are all true.  Hence wide is definitely true.  
3.  So q boils down to whether t₀ is true.  

Chaining the t‐rules:

- t₀ ← t₁  
- t₁ ← t₂  
- t₂ ← t₃  
- t₃ ← t₄  
- t₄ ← t₅  
- t₅ ← w₂  

Hence t₀ is true exactly when w₂ is true.  

Now look at w₂ and v₂:

- v₂ is true if w₂ is not true (i.e. v₂ ← ¬w₂).  
- w₂ is true if v₂ is not true (i.e. w₂ ← ¬v₂).  

These two rules make v₂ and w₂ perfect negations of each other, but nothing else pins down which side holds.  Both assignments (w₂ true, v₂ false) and (w₂ false, v₂ true) satisfy all the given rules.  Therefore w₂—and hence t₀—and hence q—can be either true or false under different (equally consistent) choices.
